Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

EL CALABOZ, Texas (CNN)  -- Eloisa Tamez said she isn't scared anymore, just determined. "I am not backing down," she said. The U.S. government wants to build a border fence like this one. About 100 landowners are fighting it. Tamez owns three acres of land along the Texas-Mexico border where the Department of Homeland Security would like to build a border fence. The property is a remnant of a 12,000-acre grant from Spain to her family in 1767, before the United States even existed. "It is my history. It is my heritage," Tamez said. This week, the Justice Department began legal action against landowners and municipalities who have refused to give government surveyors access to their land. Tamez expects she will be sued sometime soon, but she is not intimidated. Asked how long she will fight, she said, "As long as I have to." Michael Chertoff, the Secretary of Homeland Security, said the fence will not be stopped by opponents like Tamez. "Can we simply abandon an enterprise because it is a problem for a particular individual?" Chertoff told CNN. "I don't think I can accept that."  Watch Chertoff say it's "civic responsibility" to give up land » . Chertoff believes a fence would curb the steady stream of illegal immigrants making their way across the border and lessen the flow of drugs. He also argues it will increase the safety of Border Patrol agents who have faced increasing violence. The government wants to build 700 miles of fence along the Mexican border, including 370 miles of it by the end of this year. About 70 miles of fence is to be built in the Rio Grande Valley by year's end, if the government gets its way. The Rio Grande forms a natural barrier along this stretch of the border, but in some places it is narrow enough to swim across. On the banks of the river there is ample evidence that people do so. Piles of underwear lie discarded by swimmers after they make it across. The swimmers change into dry clothes they have carried across in plastic bags. Then they disappear into the United States. The Border Patrol has stepped up its efforts in the Rio Grande Valley with more lights, and sensors to pick up movement. A levee built along the river has a muddy road on top used by Border Patrol vehicles to patrol the area. Richard Cortez, the mayor of the border town of McAllen, Texas, believes hiring more Border Patrol agents, deepening the Rio Grande, and clearing its banks of tall vegetation would provide better border protection than the fence. Cortez calls the fence "a multibillion-dollar speed bump," which will slow, but not stop, illegal immigration. "It is a false sense of security," he said. "America will not be safe. America will continue to waste resources on something that is not going to work." Cortez and other border mayors who oppose construction of the fence formed a group called the Texas Border Coalition. The coalition wrote to Chertoff asking for further consultations on the fence, but this week the Department of Homeland Security turned them down. While expressing support for open dialogue with residents and officials, David Pagan of U.S. Customs and Border Protection wrote in an e-mail, "We do not plan to suspend work on the construction of fence in order to hold a series of additional consultation meetings." Cortez said his city is contemplating a court test of the law that mandated the construction of the border fence. And so a battle is being waged by about 100 landowners, those like Eloisa Tamez who are standing firm.   "I will not allow them to come and survey my land. I have an American-given right to protect my property," she said. E-mail to a friend .

outputs.L2:
**EL CALABOZ, Texas (CNN) —** Eloisa Tamez says fear has given way to resolve, and she has no intention of yielding.

Tamez owns three acres on the Texas-Mexico boundary where the Department of Homeland Security wants to erect a border fence. Her property is what remains of a 12,000-acre tract that Spain granted to her family in 1767—before the United States was founded. To Tamez, the land represents both her family’s past and her inheritance.

She is among roughly 100 property owners opposing the project. This week, the Justice Department initiated proceedings against individuals and local governments that have denied federal surveyors permission to enter their property. Tamez anticipates that she may soon face a lawsuit, but says she will resist for however long is necessary.

Homeland Security Secretary Michael Chertoff insists that objections from people such as Tamez will not derail the fence. Speaking to CNN, he argued that the government cannot abandon a major undertaking simply because it creates difficulties for a particular person. He also characterized surrendering land for the project as a “civic responsibility.”

According to Chertoff, the barrier would reduce the continuous movement of undocumented immigrants and drugs across the border. He says it would also better protect Border Patrol officers, who have encountered growing levels of violence.

Federal plans call for 700 miles of fencing along the Mexican border, with 370 miles scheduled for completion by the end of this year. If the government’s timetable prevails, approximately 70 miles will be constructed in the Rio Grande Valley before year’s end.

Although the Rio Grande itself serves as a natural boundary in this region, certain sections are narrow enough for people to swim across. Evidence of such crossings can be found along the riverbanks, including heaps of underwear abandoned by swimmers. After reaching the U.S. side, they replace their wet clothing with dry garments transported in plastic bags and then vanish into the country.

The Border Patrol has expanded its presence in the Rio Grande Valley by installing additional lighting and motion-detection sensors. Patrol vehicles also travel along a muddy road atop a levee beside the river.

McAllen Mayor Richard Cortez favors other approaches to border enforcement. He believes protection would be improved more effectively by adding Border Patrol personnel, dredging the Rio Grande to make it deeper, and removing tall plants from its banks.

Cortez describes the proposed barrier as a “multibillion-dollar speed bump”: something that might delay unauthorized crossings but would not prevent them. In his view, the fence would create only an illusion of safety, leave the country insecure, and consume public resources without producing the promised results.

Together with other border-city mayors who object to the project, Cortez helped form the Texas Border Coalition. The organization requested more discussions with Chertoff about the fence, but the Department of Homeland Security rejected that request this week.

In an email, U.S. Customs and Border Protection official David Pagan said the agency supports continued communication with local residents and government leaders. Nevertheless, he stated that construction would not be paused to conduct another round of consultation meetings.

Cortez says McAllen is considering a legal challenge to the statute requiring the border fence to be built.

Meanwhile, the dispute continues, with about 100 landowners—including Tamez—refusing to give in. She says she will deny surveyors access to her property because she believes her rights as an American allow her to defend her land.
outputs.L3:
Eloisa Tamez is resisting federal efforts to build a border fence across her three-acre property in Texas, land that has remained in her family since it was granted by the Spanish government in 1767. She is among approximately 100 Texas landowners opposing the project, many of whom are unwilling to allow government surveyors onto their property. In response, the Justice Department has begun legal action against landowners who have denied survey teams access.

Homeland Security Secretary Michael Chertoff has argued that individual objections cannot be allowed to stop a project intended to serve broader national interests. He has characterized the surrender of private land for the fence as a civic responsibility. Federal officials maintain that the barrier would help curb illegal immigration and drug trafficking while also improving safety for Border Patrol agents working along the border.

The fence is part of a larger federal plan to construct 700 miles of barriers along the U.S.–Mexico border. The government aims to complete 370 miles by the end of the year, including approximately 70 miles in Texas’s Rio Grande Valley. However, resistance from Tamez and other landowners highlights the conflict between federal border-security goals and long-standing private property rights.
outputs.L4:
The U.S. government plans to build roughly 700 miles of fencing along the Mexican border in an effort to reduce illegal immigration, drug trafficking, and border-related violence. To determine where the barriers will be placed, federal officials need access to privately owned land for surveying and construction planning. In Texas, however, some property owners have refused to allow survey crews onto their land, prompting the government to seek court orders granting temporary access.

About 100 Texas landowners are resisting the federal effort. Many argue that the proposed fencing would divide farms and communities, restrict access to the Rio Grande, and damage environmentally or culturally significant areas. They also fear that temporary survey access could be the first step toward the government acquiring portions of their property through eminent domain.

Among those challenging the plan is Eloisa Tamez, whose family has held land near the border for generations. Tamez views the property not simply as real estate but as part of her family’s history and cultural identity. She has opposed federal attempts to enter the land, arguing that the government should not be able to override ancestral ownership without meaningful consultation and adequate legal protections.

Federal officials maintain that the surveys are necessary to evaluate proposed fence routes and that stronger physical barriers are an important part of border security. They say the fencing is intended to help law-enforcement agencies control heavily traveled crossing areas and combat smuggling and violence. When owners deny access, the government can turn to the courts and, if necessary, use eminent-domain authority to obtain land for public purposes while providing compensation.

The dispute illustrates a broader conflict between national security policy and private property rights. Supporters of the fence emphasize the federal government’s responsibility to secure the border, while opponents question the project’s effectiveness and its impact on residents whose families have lived in the region for decades or even centuries. For landowners such as Tamez, the fight is therefore about more than compensation: it is about preserving family heritage, local communities, and the right to control ancestral land.
